title: Structured coherent thermal emission from non-Hermitian metasurfaces

paper_content.abstract: Metasurfaces can reshape thermal radiation with tailored directionality, spectral selectivity and polarization control, yet coherent thermal emission exhibiting vectorial polarization or structured light property has been rarely demonstrated. Here, we introduce a non-Hermitian thermal meta-emitter that experimentally generates highly directional, rainbow-free, vectorial-polarized thermal emission. Through perturbation-induced Brillouin-zone folding, we couple high-radiative-loss Fabry–Pérot modes to symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum and exploit non-Hermitian dynamics near exceptional points to achieve simultaneous dispersion and loss engineering. This yields a sharp variation of the radiative Q-factor in k-space, flexibly triggering vectorial-polarized emissions only at selected output angles. Experimental studies reveal doughnut-shaped narrowband thermal emission in the 3–5 μm atmospheric transparency window, exhibiting high spectral purity, extreme directionality and distinct vectorial polarizations. Our design establishes a powerful non-Hermitian platform to sculpt incoherent thermal fluctuations into coherent vectorial-polarized beams at a specific frequency, overcoming trade-offs in coherence, spectral selectivity and polarization control.
paper_content.introduction:
As a ubiquitous electromagnetic radiation phenomenon in nature, the physical essence of thermal radiation stems from the random thermal fluctuations of charges within any object whose temperature exceeds absolute zero. Within the framework of classical thermodynamics, thermal radiation typically exhibits broadband, omnidirectional, and incoherent, and unpolarized characteristics, a traditional understanding that has been perfectly encapsulated in the laws of blackbody radiation and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. However, recent groundbreaking advancements in nanophotonic and metamaterial technologies are reshaping this fundamental physical landscape1–6. Through the meticulous design of artificial micro- and nanostructures, researchers have successfully achieved precise control over multiple dimensions of thermal emissions (ThE), including spectral, spatial, and polarization, manifesting extraordinary properties such as narrow linewidths, high directionality and controllable polarization states7–12.

This revolutionary concept of “taming thermal fluctuations” not only deepens the foundational understanding of non-equilibrium thermodynamics but also heralds transformative technological opportunities in critical fields such as infrared sensing13,14, thermophotovoltaics15,16, and radiative cooling17,18.

The mid-infrared (MIR) band is widely recognized as the molecular fingerprint region, making ThE with temporal/spatial coherence19,20 and polarization control as a light source particularly appealing. By coupling thermal fluctuations to optical structures that support high-quality (Q) factors, selective spectral components of thermal radiation can be directionally guided into free space, thereby achieving highly coherent ThE. This process is akin to transforming chaotic thermal fluctuations into a harmonious symphony, where each photon is in phase with its neighbors. Recent advances have demonstrated the use of nonlocal metasurfaces21, which exhibits substantial interactions between adjacent meta-atoms to produce high-Q responses, in the flexible reshaping of ThE with high coherence19,22. In terms of polarization control, optical modes such as surface phonon polaritons3, localized surface plasmon resonances23,24, and Mie resonances25 in dielectric structures have been extensively utilized for linearly polarized ThE26–29. Recent breakthroughs in circularly polarized ThE have also provided unique prospects for applications such as circular dichroism infrared sensing and chiral molecule detection9,30–37. Meanwhile, a vectorial-polarized beam, with its rich and unique polarization state distributions (including radial and azimuthal polarizations), has demonstrated great potential in fields such as focused imaging, particle trapping, and laser processing38–41. However, to date, these exotic polarization states have predominantly been achieved by relying on the synergistic effects of external laser sources and bulky optical components, such as spatial light modulators. In contrast, the control of vectorial-polarized ThE using thermal emitters remains a significantly underexplored area of research. Although metal-insulator-metal absorbing metasurfaces can endow individual meta-atoms with tailored polarization states to yield vectorial-polarized ThE, the inherent plasmonic losses severely degrade temporal coherence. To the best of our knowledge, vectorial-polarized or any other form of structured ThE with high temporal coherence (Q > 50) has been scarcely demonstrated. While Zhang et al. recently reported the realization of polarization vortices in ThE42, their system maintains near-critical coupling over a broad range of wavevectors and wavelengths. The persistence of this critical coupling condition along the dispersive BIC band (Fig. 1a) inevitably leads to broad emission angles and the characteristic rainbow effect. In contrast, our non-Hermitian approach enables us to confine the critical coupling state to a specific, narrow angular and spectral window (Fig. 1b). This ensures highly directional, rainbow-free, doughnut-shaped vectorial-polarized ThE, which is essential for meeting the demands of practical applications.

Furthermore, as open systems, thermal emitters can benefit from the rich physical phenomena supported by non-Hermitian descriptions43,44. To date, most studies on their intriguing results have focused on systems that rely on material loss and gain. These systems exhibit parity-time (PT) symmetry and demonstrate optical phase transitions at exceptional points (EPs) between weak and strong coupling regimes45,46. Near an EP, the Hilbert space of the system becomes severely “skewed”, rendering the system’s dynamical behavior highly sensitive to minute perturbations. This sensitivity provides an effective approach for designing and controlling thermal emitters with extreme spatial and spectral properties.

In this work, by leveraging the non-Hermitian engineering in nonlocal metasurfaces, we have designed and implemented a four-hole unit cell structure, through which we successfully realize two types of highly directional, rainbow-free, and doughnut-shaped coherent ThE featuring vectorial polarizations. Specifically, topological charge engineering induced by Brillouin zone folding (BZF) enables flexible triggering of vectorial polarization states at the Γ point. By simultaneously tuning the distances among the four holes, a four-level coupled-mode system is constructed. In this system, high-radiative-loss Fabry–Pérot (FP) modes are strategically coupled to the symmetry-protected BIC, and the complete coupling evolution is demonstrated. During this process, we observe the formation, annihilation, and reformation of EPs and EP-induced band loops, without requiring any artificial optical gain. A pair of BIC-based mini-flatbands emerges as intermediate states during this dynamic process. Furthermore, the non-Hermitian interaction near EPs induces sharp variations in radiative loss with wavevector k, which enables critical coupling between radiation and material absorption losses only at specific k-values—thereby maximizing emissivity with high directionality and suppressing the rainbow effect that plagues conventional dispersive systems whose Q factor depends weakly on k. Away from these k-points, a mismatch between these two loss rates leads to a sharp drop in emissivity, a characteristic inherited by the double-BIC mini-flatband design. Leveraging these unique non-Hermitian physical mechanisms, we theoretically and experimentally demonstrate doughnut-shaped vectorial-polarized ThE with simultaneously high spectral purity and extreme directionality. These remarkable and unconventional results open up new possibilities for on-chip laser-like thermal sources in applications such as infrared photonic manipulation and high-fidelity thermal imaging.
paper_content.results:
Figure 1a, b schematically compare the ThE characteristics between a traditional dispersive system and a mini-flatband counterpart engineered via non-Hermitian strategies. Both systems support symmetry-protected BICs, which are characterized by infinite Q-factors and integer topological charges in momentum space47–49. However, traditional BIC systems typically exhibit dispersive behavior, and the radiation Q factor (Qrad) usually exhibits two distinct dependencies on k as it deviates from the BIC point50. Initially, Qrad is highly sensitive to changes in k, but it becomes less sensitive as k moves away (see also Fig. S2c). According to the temporal coupled-mode theory (TCMT), the emissivity of the entire system can be determined by the contrast between the absorption and radiation losses7. Perfect absorption (PA) or emission (PE) is achieved under the critical coupling condition Qrad ≈ Qabs, where Qabs is the absorption Q factor. Therefore, for a given intrinsic absorption loss, the control of radiative loss provides additional flexibility in tuning emissivity. The weak dependence of Qrad on k where k > kBIC50, combined with the moderate value of the absorption Q factor (Qabs) in lossy ThE systems, suggests that near-critical coupling conditions can be sustained in the second region over a broad wavevector range. These features result in high emissivity distributed over wide angular spans at frequencies determined by the dispersion band42,51, which is known as the rainbow effect, as illustrated in the bottom panel of Fig. 1a. Consequently, although conventional architectures based on dispersive BIC modes can facilitate the generation of vectorial polarizations in ThE42, they typically exhibit broadband critical coupling behavior. In such systems, high emissivity persists across a wide range of angles as the resonance wavelength shifts, necessitating the use of auxiliary ultra-narrowband filters with omnidirectional responses to achieve precise spectral selection. However, this approach is complex and significantly complicates integration into practical platforms, such as on-chip thermal light sources. In contrast, the mini-flatband system, designed through band and dissipation engineering—specifically by tailoring radiative loss to induce a phase-transition-like critical coupling behavior at small wavevectors—addresses the above challenges. Within this mini-flatband, Qrad remains at moderate values, which are necessary to fulfill the critical coupling, while keeping its high sensitivity to k (see Fig. S2c). As a result, it supports high ThE at a single central frequency across a narrow angular range (see Fig. 1b). Since the mini-flatbands are close to the Γ point (where a BIC with surrounding vortex features in polarizations is located), the system enables highly directional, rainbow-free, doughnut-shaped ThE directly in real space, eliminating the need for additional spectral/spatial filtering. Figure 1c illustrates the working principle of the final thermal emitter designed in this work. The yellow bottom layer represents a sufficiently thick gold film. When the whole structure is heated by applying an electric current across the gold film or placed in a high-temperature environment, thermal fluctuations will be provided that couple into the resonant modes of the upper structure, thereby radiating vectorial-polarized ThE into free space. Here, we present two types of vectorial polarization states: a superposition of radial and azimuthal polarizations carrying a −1 topological charge (left panel of Fig. 1c) and a pure azimuthally polarized state carrying a +1 topological charge (right panel). Besides the vectorial polarizations, the achieved emissions exhibit strong intensity confined to the doughnut ring and rapid suppression at both the center and outer periphery. The flexibility in controlling the vectorial features of ThE holds promise for emerging applications such as high-resolution thermal imaging and target identification.

The above properties stem from the integrated use of non-Hermitian engineering, including topological, band, and dissipation control mechanisms (see Fig. S2 for more details). Figure 2 systematically demonstrates the details of this engineering process. We begin with a meticulously designed partially-etched metasurface structure, whose geometric parameters are shown in Fig. 2a. The top layer is a high-refractive-index Ge film (n = 4.16) with a total thickness of 495 nm, serving to support required guided modes (GMs). A periodic array of circular air holes, with a carefully chosen period of a = 800 nm and radius of r = 195 nm, is partially etched into the Ge layer, leaving an ultrathin slab with a remaining thickness of h = 125 nm. The entire structure, including the patterned layer and the slab, supports both GM and FP modes at the target frequency. A low-index ZnS layer (n = 2.22) with a thickness of t = 865 nm is inserted between the Ge and the Au layer, which mainly helps separate the metasurface from the metal to reduce the impact of the inherent loss of Au52. We numerically calculate the band structures supported by this system using the finite element method (FEM) implemented in the commercial software COMSOL Multiphysics. As shown in Fig. 2b, the structure supports a series of GMs with infinite Q-factors below the light line (yellow region), as well as FP modes (green dashed lines) that couple into free space via the light cone interface. The GMs of interest along the Γ→X and Γ→M directions are labeled GMA, GMC, and GMB in blue, orange, and red, respectively.

To enable the coupling of these GMs to free space, we designed a four-hole unit-cell metasurface to induce bidirectional band folding, as illustrated in Fig. 2d. By introducing a perturbation δ in the positions of four adjacent holes along both the x and y-directions, the first Brillouin zone (FBZ) shrinks because of the length doubling of the unit cell along each direction, which now includes four holes (Fig. 2e). This operation causes the GMs originally below the light cone and at the FBZ boundary to fold into the continuum, forming QGMs50,53,54. When δ = 20 nm, the band structure supported by the metasurface is shown in Fig. 2e, where the color-coded folded bands originate from the corresponding GMs in Fig. 2b. The field distributions in Fig. S3 demonstrate one-to-one correspondence between GMs and QGMs. Importantly, in the unperturbed structure, these GMs lie entirely below the light cone and therefore carry zero topological charge. In contrast, for the bidirectionally band-folded metasurface, the C4v symmetry of the structure leads to the formation of symmetry-protected BICs for the QGMA and QGMB modes at the Γ point (see Fig. S11). Under the constraint of topological charge conservation, these two modes acquire customizable topological charges of −1 and +1, respectively, which give rise to distinct textures of vectorial polarizations in their surrounding momentum space, as shown in Fig. 2f. This topological engineering thus lays a crucial foundation for the realization of tailored vectorial-polarized ThE.

It is noteworthy that this four-hole configuration bears a structural resemblance to second-order topological photonic crystals55–57. However, a fundamental distinction lies in the operational regime: while those topological systems typically function below the light cone to host localized corner or edge states, our design leverages out-of-plane radiation above the light cone. This shift into the radiative regime introduces unique non-Hermitian opportunities; specifically, the interplay between topological lattice symmetries, exceptional points and wavevector-sensitive radiative losses enables the realization of highly directional, rainbow-free ThE. Such dynamics represent a significant extension of the functionality usually explored in the context of second-order topological physics. By investigating the radiative properties of topological metasurfaces, our approach bridges the gap between topological photonics and non-Hermitian thermal photonics, opening new avenues for the development of structured, coherent thermal radiations sources.

In order to elucidate the rich physics arising from near-field coupling between different modes and their influence on radiation losses, we assume zero material absorption loss, modeling an ideal open system. We consider only four interacting modes near the Γ-point: QGMA, QGMB, QGMC, and FP. In this gain-free system, we accurately track the band and dissipation evolution by varying δ. The states of QGMA and QGMB at the Γ point are marked as BICA and BICB, as shown in Fig. 2g. The near-zero imaginary part of the complex eigen frequency and its inverse-quadratic dependence on k confirm their BIC nature (Q factor results, see Fig. S15). In addition, these two modes are coupled with each other near the Γ-point under the introduction of δ. It should be noted that at smaller δ values, the FP mode is far from the high-frequency QGM band. Overall, this results in robust and large imaginary parts of the complex eigenfrequencies, which corresponds to small Qrad. As δ increases, QGMA and QGMB move toward lower frequencies, while the FP mode shifts in the reversed direction. These spectral shifts enable a crossing and interaction between the FP mode and QGMA, as shown in Fig. 2i. Energy exchange occurs in three modes around k ~ 0.035π/a, resulting in a significant increase in the imaginary parts of QGMA and QGMB eigenfrequencies, while the imaginary parts of FP eigen frequencies are significantly suppressed. As δ further increases, the FP mode crosses over QGMB and intercalates between QGMA and QGMB. At δ = 165.6 nm, the interaction between QGMB and FP modes lead to the formation of EPs and significant non-Hermitian EP-induced band loop behavior near the Γ point.

To describe this phenomenon, we employ the TCMT to outline the theoretical framework of the system. Further details of this model are provided in Section 3 of the Supplemental Information (SI). We initially consider the coupling between four modes—QGMA, QGMB, QGMC and FP—using a 4×4 Hamiltonian. As δ increases, we observe a clear phenomenon of EP and EP-induced band loop formation, annihilation, and reformation. When δ approaches certain critical values, the coupling between two of the four modes becomes dominant. Consequently, the Hamiltonian can be simplified to a 2×2 model. At critical coupling conditions, which correspond to the δ values of 165.6 nm and 198 nm, the two eigenvalues of the 2×2 Hamiltonian coalesce into one. This coalesce involves both the resonant frequency and the leakage rates merging simultaneously, signifying the formation of an EP. Furthermore, the real and imaginary parts of the complex eigenfrequencies exhibit a ring-liked distribution in the vicinity of the Γ point (see Fig. 2i and k).

More importantly, during this process, the interplay among the four modes results in distinct topological features. At δ = 173 nm, two mini-flatbands carrying topological charges emerge near the Γ point (the 2D band structure and group velocity are shown in Fig. S4), retaining the unique characteristics induced by the EP effect, such as the steep variation of radiation loss with wavevector, as shown in Fig. 2j. In real devices where one needs to consider the material absorption of the system, there is a fast mismatch between radiation loss and absorption loss as the wavevector deviates from a certain k. The QGMC and FP modes exhibit extremely low Q factors as weakened radiation backgrounds. The radiation loss of two mini-flatbands supporting BIC is significantly enhanced on the EP-induced band loop formed before and after controlling δ and undergoes a phase transition near the EPs. These common behaviors not only ensure the rapid achievement and mismatch of critical coupling but also ensure that it only occurs at a single center output frequency. This is the key to achieve rainbow-free effect in real space and doughnut-shaped ThE with vectorial polarizations.

We conducted numerical simulations of the structure based on the final geometric design, incorporating realistic absorption losses to validate its ThE characteristics. According to Kirchhoff’s law of thermal radiation, the emissivity and absorptivity of an object in thermal equilibrium are equivalent. Consequently, the emissivity can be characterized by the calculated absorptivity of the structure, i.e., E(λ) = A(λ) = 1 − R(λ) − T(λ). Due to the optically thick bottom layer of gold, which prevents light transmission (T(λ) = 0; experimental transmission spectra are shown in Fig. S14), this expression simplifies to E(λ) = A(λ) = 1 − R(λ). For comparison, we first designed a conventional metasurface with C4v point group symmetry that supports BIC modes with a dispersive band, as illustrated in the right panel of Fig. 3a. This metasurface supports an azimuthal far-field polarization distribution near the Γ point (see Fig. S12 for more details). The material composition of this system is identical to that of the metasurface. The geometric parameters are assumed to be a = 1600 nm, h = 485 nm, and t = 500 nm. To simplify calculations, the imaginary parts of the refractive indices of Ge and ZnS are both assumed to be 0.002, closely approximating experimental values for evaporated Ge/ZnS materials in the MIR. The left panel of Fig. 3a presents the calculated total Q (Qtotal), Qrad and Qabs factors as a function of the emission angle for this conventional BIC system with a dispersive band. The angle-resolved ThE spectrum under y-polarization in the Γ→X direction is shown in Fig. 3b. Due to the infinite Qrad of the BIC, the emissivity at the Γ point is nearly zero. As the emission angle increases, the spectrum exhibits significant dispersion, and the emissivity gradually increases, reaching its maximum at approximately θ ~ 13°. However, because Qrad and Qabs remain nearly critically coupled over a broad angular range, the system maintains a relatively high emissivity over an angular range as wide as 20° (emissivity > 0.75), which aligns well with the theoretical explanation in Fig. 1a. Figure 3c, d show the calculated Qtotal, Qrad, and Qabs as a function of the emission angle for the structure with δ = 173 nm, corresponding to the two mini-flatband systems. The slight variation of Qabs with wavevector arises from the electric field mode distribution changes induced by the EP. Notably, the sharp variation in Qrad leads to a rapid mismatch with Qabs, resulting in higher contrast. Figure 3e illustrates the angle-resolved ThE spectrum in the Γ→X direction for y-polarized light under these geometric parameters. The two mini-flatbands located at 4.797 μm and 4.691 μm correspond to QGMB and QGMA in Fig. 3c, d, respectively. The near-zero emissivity at the Γ point is supported by the vortex characteristics of BICB and BICA on the mini-flatbands. It is noteworthy that due to the rapid variation of Qrad on the two mini-flatbands of BICB and BICA, critical coupling with Qabs occurs at emission angles as small as 1.2° and 1.42°, respectively, attaining near-unity emissivity. It is important to note that both systems exhibit Qrad with a k−2 decay sharpness, as shown in Fig. S7. However, our method is able to reduce the wavevector distance between the critical coupling position and the Γ point by approximately one order of magnitude. This represents an approximately one order of magnitude reduction in the emission angle where critical coupling occurs. As the emission angle further increases, the rapid decrease of Qrad and the resulting deviation from the critical coupling condition lead to a sharp decline in emissivity, thereby effectively suppressing ThE at large angles and at other wavelengths (for detailed comparative results over a wider angular range, see Fig. S6). For comparison, we also designed a merged BIC58 thermal emitter that supports a k−6 sharpness, as shown in Fig. S8. Clearly, this system exhibits an infinitely large Qrad factor over a broader wavevector range, approximately three orders of magnitude higher than in our work, resulting in the critical coupling position occurring at larger angles. These results highlight the enhanced versatility of our approach in achieving small divergence angles, high directionality, and high-purity doughnut-shaped coherent vectorial-polarized ThE, while avoiding the broad angular dispersion in emission output.

We employ the topological charge of polarization singularities48 to extract more information on the BICs within the mini-flatbands. Calculations of the topological charge can be found in Section 4 of the SI. By calculating the far-field polarization vector fields of QGMB and QGMA near the Γ point, we observe in Fig. 3f, h that BICB, carrying a topological charge of +1, exhibits an azimuthally polarized far-field distribution (detailed numerical results for a broader wavevector range are provided in Fig. S9). In contrast, BICA, carrying a topological charge of −1, displays an azimuthal polarization along the kx and ky directions but radial polarization along a 45°-rotated axis. The momentum-space ThE patterns of the two modes are presented in Fig. 3g, i. These results confirm that the polarization vortex distribution induced by topological charge-carrying BICs, in conjunction with mini-flatband formation and dissipation engineering, lead to rainbow-free ThE exhibiting distinct doughnut-shaped beams with vectorial polarizations—fully consistent with the expected description in Fig. 1.

Based on the above design, we fabricated such a thermal emitter with δ = 173 nm using standard nanofabrication techniques (see Fig. S1 for more details of the fabrication processes). Figure 4a, b presents the top-view and cross-sectional pseudo-color scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of the fabricated structure, demonstrating high processing accuracy. Figure 4c illustrates a schematic of the custom-built setup for the characterization of ThE. The sample is mounted on a 3D-controllable rotating stage equipped with a heating system, allowing precise multidimensional adjustments to measure ThE at different azimuthal and output angles. Two coaxial apertures (JCOPTIX, China), placed between the sample and a rotatable linear polarizer (JCOPTIX, China), significantly reduce background emission and enhance the accuracy of angle-resolved ThE measurements. The collected ThE is analyzed using a Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer equipped with a mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector.

By heating the sample to 200°C, we conducted precise angle-resolved ThE measurements at different azimuthal and polarization angles. As shown in the inset of Fig. 4c, the emission spectrum was recorded at different azimuthal angles (β) by rotating the stage with respect to the surface normal direction. Angle-resolved emission spectra were then obtained by rotating the stage within a fixed plane containing the z-axis, thus controlling the emission angle θ. The polarization property was characterized by rotating the polarizer at fixed values of θ and β. Due to the structure’s high C4v point group symmetry, we measured the emissions spectra at different azimuthal angles (β = 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 180°, 202.5°, and 225°) and the results are presented in Fig. 5a–c (the corresponding numerical results are presented in Fig. S5). The color amplitude represents the intensity of ThE. All the results in Fig. 5a correspond to the case of β = 0 (see the left panel of Fig. 5a). The middle panel of Fig. 5a displays the angle-resolved ThE spectrum within the xz plane under y-polarization (α = 90°), where the emissivity center wavelengths are fitted by dashed lines corresponding to the theoretical predictions in Fig. 2j. Notably, the two mini-flatbands with output wavelengths of 4.84 and 4.705 μm exhibit near-zero emissivity in the normal direction. As the emission angle increases, the intensity first rises rapidly and then decreases sharply, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. In Fig. S13, we present the measured emission spectrum at the output angle of θ = 2°. The fitting results show that the two modes exhibit Q-factors of 97 and 73, corresponding to bandwidths of 50 nm and 64 nm, respectively. These values indicate relatively high temporal coherence. It should be noted that the experimentally observed critical coupling angle is slightly larger than the simulation results, and the measured Q-factors are slightly lower. This discrepancy is attributed to unavoidable multi-angle collection during the measurement process and additional scattering losses induced by sidewall roughness. The right panel of Fig. 5a presents the angle-resolved ThE spectrum under x-polarization (α = 0°) within the xz plane, where the weak emission feature near 4.63 μm corresponds to an x-polarized FP mode. The presence of mini-flatband and high-intensity ThE for y-polarization and the absence of these features for x-polarization confirm that these modes exhibit azimuthal polarization at β = 0. Considering the C4v symmetry of the structure, the same behavior repeatedly occurs at β = 90, 180 and 270°. The measurement results presented in Fig. 5b, obtained at β = 22.5°, show that the QGMB and QGMA modes reach maximum emission intensities at the polarization angles of α = 112.5° and 67.5°, respectively. This indicates that QGMB maintains azimuthal polarization, while QGMA gradually transitions toward radial polarization. The middle panel of Fig. 5c presents the results obtained at β = 45°, revealing that QGMB achieves maximum emission at α = 135°. This confirms that the QGMB mode maintains azimuthal polarization throughout the entire radiation space, consistent with the C4v symmetry of the structure. In contrast, the right panel of Fig. 5c shows that the QGMA mode achieves peak emission at α = 45°, indicating that its emission alternates between azimuthal and radial polarization at 45° intervals in radiation space. These experimental results are in excellent agreement with the simulations in Fig. 3 and Fig. S5. It should be noted that the slight asymmetry observed in the angle-resolved ThE measurements in Fig. 5 can be attributed to a combination of experimental factors. Primarily, minor optical misalignment—specifically, a slight tilt of the sample relative to the optical axis during the angle-resolved capture—induces the observed intensity deviations between symmetric wavevectors. Additionally, fabrication imperfections, such as sidewall roughness and minor defects in the metasurface structure, may introduce non-uniform scattering losses.

To further visualize the spatial ThE patterns of the two modes, we measured and mapped the ThE intensity in momentum space at the two mini-flatband wavelengths. Figure 5d illustrates the measured azimuthal polarization dependence for QGMB, which exhibits peak emissivity at 4.84 μm and clearly shows a characteristic doughnut-shaped azimuthal polarization distribution in momentum space. The polarization ratio of the x and y components of the emissivity, with respect to the azimuthal angle β, follows the relation (sin β, −cos β). This phenomenon is easily associated with real space scenarios, where the ThE associated with QGMB resonance exhibits azimuthally polarized response, with rainbow-free and highly directional behaviors. The doughnut radius varies with the observation distance, consistent with the schematic in Fig. 1c. Figure 5e presents the emissivity associated with QGMA resonance in momentum space, demonstrating a polarization ratio given by (sin β, cos β). Unlike QGMB, QGMA exhibits azimuthal polarization along the x and y-axes but also radial polarization along the 45° direction. These experimental results, summarized in the right panels of Fig. 5d and e, show excellent agreement with the numerical predictions in Fig. 3g, i, and Fig. S10a, c. We also calculated the angular emission distribution for different polarization angles α, as shown in Fig. S10b, d, which further validates our experimental findings. Importantly, a single thermal emitter can simultaneously generate vectorial-polarized ThE at two distinct wavelengths with different characteristics, offering significant potential for diverse on-chip light source applications.
paper_content.methods:
Numerical simulations
All numerical simulations were performed based on the FEM using the commercial software of COMSOL Multiphysics. Floquet periodic boundary conditions were implemented in the lateral directions of a unit cell to define the wavevectors, while PML was employed in the z direction to mimic a non-reflecting infinite domain.

Fabrication
First, a 5-nm-thick adhesion layer of Ti, a 100-nm-thick Au film and another 3-nm-thick Ti were successively deposited onto a Si substrate using electron beam evaporation. After that, two layers of 865 nm ZnS and 495 nm Ge were deposited onto the sample using the same equipment. Then, the 180-nm-thick PMMA resist layer was spin coated onto the sample and the reverse-designed structure pattern was exposed onto the PMMA layer by an electron beam lithography system. After developing, 20 nm Al was evaporated onto the sample, and the lift-off process was used to transfer the pattern from PMMA to the Al layer. The Al pattern worked as a mask to obtain the Ge structure in a subsequent inductively coupled plasma-enhanced reaction ion etching process. Finally, the residual Al was completely removed by soaking the sample in NaOH solution.

Optical measurements
The emissivity of the fabricated samples was measured using a Fourier transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR) (Bruker Vertex 80V) equipped with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector. The emissivity measurements were carried out by loading the sample onto an emission adapter (Bruker, A540), which was employed to heat the sample at different temperatures to induce thermal emissions. Steel plates of the same size, blackened by the black soot of candles, were used as the standard blackbody reference. Both the blackbody and the fabricated sample were loaded onto the heating plate. When the blackbody and the sample were heated to 200°C, the emitted power was sent to the FTIR system and detected by the MCT detector. The thicknesses of the different films were measured using a Mueller matrix ellipsometer (ME-L ellipsometer, Wuhan Eoptics Technology Co., Wuhan, China).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this work, the authors experimentally demonstrate vector beams generated through thermal emission using a multi-mode non-Hermitian engineering approach. This experimental work is timely with recent theoretical works on shaping non-Hermitian bands [10.1103/378r-pmcv]. While the paper is well written and clear, I cannot recommend publication in Nature Communications as I have major technical questions that must be addressed before publication. With satisfactory changes to the manuscript, I am happy to recommend publication.
Major:
1. What are the advantages of this method over engineering the sharpness of the BIC fall-off, i.e. going from 1/k^2 to 1/k^6 using approaches demonstrated in [10.1038/s41586-019-1664-7]?
2. What happens to the polarization charges of the exceptional points at 150 nm and 173 nm? Did the singularities move outside the zone shown in Fig. 3f,h (|k|>0.03)? Do they collide with other charges?
3. What does Fig. 3e look like from -20 degrees to +20 degrees? It looks like decently strong thermal emission should be observed for QGMa since the Q-factor increases from a minimum of 40 to 200 which is only a factor of 5 off the critical coupling condition. This should be very close to the +20-degree case for "Traditional BICs."
4. All the experimental emission plots are presented in relative emissivity with arbitrary units. True emissivity needs to be reported so readers can understand expected performance levels for this type of non-Hermitian engineering of thermal emitters.
5. What is the polarizer angle (alpha) in Fig. 5d and e? Moreover, why is the expected polarization behavior so hard to observe? From Fig. 5d, I do not see the near zero intensity I would expect from Fig. 5a with a polarization angle of 0 degrees. The experimental evidence is not clear proof of the expected polarization distribution and the existence of vector beams. Can the authors explain why the behavior in Fig. 5a,b,c is so different from that in Fig. 5d,e?
6. In the SI, Fig. S3 uses electric field amplitudes which obscures the characters of the modes. Plotting the appropriate field components for TE and TM like modes would greatly clarify for the reader which modes are used.
Minor:
1. Line 381, Eps. should be EPs.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The present manuscript reported the design, theoretical analysis, and experimental demonstration of a non-Hermitian thermal metasurface capable of generating highly directional, rainbow-free, coherent thermal emission with vectorial polarization states. The authors introduced a nonlocal metasurface composed of a patterned Ge membrane atop a ZnS spacer and thin gold film. By applying Brillouin-zone folding and non-Hermitian mode engineering, they hybridized Fabry–Perot modes with quasi-guided modes, leading to the couple of symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum (BICs). Through carefully tuning the perturbation parameter, the system undergoes exceptional point (EP) formation, annihilation, and reformation, leading to the emergence of topological mini-flatbands that feature steep, wavevector-sensitive radiative loss. These bands enable critical coupling at narrowly defined angles while suppressing emission elsewhere. The authors demonstrated experimentally the doughnut-shaped vectorial-polarized thermal emission modes within the 3–5 um window, achieving Q-factors up to ~100 and strong directional confinement.
The results are solid in both theory and experiment. The work presents a notable conceptual and technological advance in thermal meta-photonics by integrating non-Hermitian physics, BIC engineering, and dissipation control. generate. The demonstration of highly coherent structured thermal radiation will be one step closer for the potential applications in infrared optical manipulation and micro-scale thermal imaging. I will strongly recommend for reconsideration in Nature Communications, if the authors can address my concerns accordingly.
(1) The four-hole unit-cell metasurface used in this work could be related to second-order topological photonic crystal [e.g. Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 233902 (2019), Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 233903 (2019), Optica 6, 786-789 (2019)], which are operating below light cone, while this work focuses on the out-of-plane intriguing radiation above light cone. I encourage the authors to give detailed discussions on these two topics that will broaden the research interests for nanophotonic community.
(2) The wording ‘bilayer metasurface’ should be seriously reconsidered. Generally, ‘bilayer metasurface’ is patterned with subwavelength meta-structures in the both two layers.
(3) The 4*4 effective Hamiltonian of TCMT contains substantial physics effects, and the authors developed a specific case of 2*2 model to discuss EP band. Can the Hamiltonian be developed another case for BIC band or mini flat band?
(4) I am confused about the role of thick gold film, the yellow bottom layer shown in Fig. 1c. Moreover, the details of COMSOL simulation setup should be added (e.g. the absorption loss of gold film), so that it will make others repeat the simulation results.
(5) What is the definition of emissivity, and how to evaluate the emissivity value of traditional BIC in Fig. 3a? How about the emissivity value of QGM_B [Fig. 3c] and QGM_A [Fig. 3d]?
(6) Traditional BIC has a trend that Q_rad is proportional to 1/|k|^2. I’m curious about the Q-k trends of QGM_B [Fig. 3c] and QGM_A [Fig. 3d].
(7) Some minor issues that confuse me, and may also confuse other readers.
7.1 In Line 313 of manuscript, what is the meaning of Gamma-X-z plane?
7.2 In Line 91 of supplementary material, the expression of phi(k) may be misunderstanding whether the term arg[…] should be included in the denominator or numerator.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, Sun et al. report the realization of polarization vortices within a thermal emitter, discussing the application of non-Hermitian engineering to control thermal emission. Leveraging topological concepts for thermal management is a timely pursuit, with potential implications for thermophotovoltaics and radiative cooling. Specifically, the authors focus on Bound States in the Continuum (BIC)-induced polarization vortices, utilizing non-Hermitian physics to manipulate dispersion and emissivity.
While the subject matter is undeniably interesting, I have some reservations regarding the novelty of the reported findings and the sufficiency of the experimental data to support the central claims. Therefore, I cannot recommend publication in its current form. I would be willing to reconsider my decision only after the authors have adequately addressed the major concerns detailed below.
Major Comments：
1. Novelty and relationship to Ref. 46: Ref. 46 has already demonstrated polarization vortices in thermal emission. In the introduction, the authors imply that such vortex emission has not been realized, which is not accurate. The authors should fairly acknowledge the prior work and clearly state what additional physics or capabilities the present work provides beyond Ref. 46. Besides, in my opinion, achieving a high Q factor for thermal emission at longer wavelengths is more challenging; therefore, it is not fair to emphasize the Q factor here, given that Ref. 46 operates at much longer wavelengths (>10 um) compared with the present work (~5 um), and the measured Q factor in this work is also not particularly high.
2. Evidence for the "mini-flat band": From Fig. 2, the band in panel (j) does not appear significantly flatter than that in (g). I suggest providing quantitative evidence (e.g., group velocity) to substantiate this claim. Additionally, a 2D band structure plot would help support the claim better.
3. Critical coupling and spectral signatures: The numerical results show critical coupling occurring within a narrow bandwidth, but this feature is not clearly visible in the emission spectrum. As perfect absorption is typically used to identify critical coupling, can the authors measure transmission and reflection to confirm this? Also, the dispersion shown in Fig. 2 (including real and imaginary parts) could likely be extracted using the same experimental setup, which would strengthen the manuscript.
4. Quality of experimental data (Fig. 5): The measured emission appears asymmetric, especially in Fig. 5(b). The authors should explain why this occurs—is it due to fabrication deviations or measurement misalignment? Furthermore, the polarization plots in (d) and (e) seem to be numerical rather than experimental. Since the polarization vortex is a key result of this work, experimental validation is needed.
Minor Issues：
1.The phrase “convert incoherent thermal fluctuations into coherent vectorial-polarized beams” is inaccurate. Vectorial-polarized beams generally imply stable phase relationships in different directions, but thermal emission is inherently incoherent with random phase. Unless the authors provide experimental evidence demonstrating directional phase coherence, this statement should be revised.
2.I think it is better to show the numerically calculated dispersion in Fig. 5(b) and (c) for direct comparison.
3.In Fig. 2(b), how is the angle-resolved emission spectrum computed? Is it actually calculated from the absorption spectrum? Please clarify.
4.Colorbars in Fig. S4 of the Supplementary Information are missing.

Response to Reviewers’ Comments
In this document the reviewers' comments are pasted in blue, our response in black and the parts newly added to the manuscript are in red.
Reply to Reviewer #1
Reviewer #1:
In this work, the authors experimentally demonstrate vector beams generated through thermal emission
using a multi-mode non-Hermitian engineering approach. This experimental work is timely with recent
theoretical works on shaping non-Hermitian bands [10.1103/378r-pmcv]. While the paper is well
written and clear, I cannot recommend publication in Nature Communications as I have major technical
questions that must be addressed before publication. With satisfactory changes to the manuscript, I am
happy to recommend publication.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful and constructive comments on our
manuscript, and we are encouraged by the positive feedback regarding the clarity and quality of the
paper.
We also thank the reviewer for providing the important reference [10.103/378r-pmcv], which has
significantly informed our revision. In that theoretical work, the authors introduced an elegant effective
Hamiltonian model to describe the key physical characteristics of exceptional points (EPs) and bulk
Fermi arcs (BFAs), systematically investigating how the position of EPs and the associated BFAs
depend on the type and degree of symmetry breaking in the 2D unit cell.
While both studies leverage non-Hermitian engineering to manipulate dispersion and losses, our work
differs in several key aspects and focuses on different physical objectives. Unlike the symmetry-
breaking approach employed in the cited work, we first achieve topological BICs with opposite charges
through band folding, while maintaining the C symmetry of the structure. By controlling the coupling
4V
between multiple modes with a single geometric parameter, we realize the formation, annihilation, and
re-formation of EPs and EP-induced band loop. During this process, we generate two mini-flatbands
with opposite topological charges. Importantly, we demonstrate experimentally how non-Hermitian
engineering can reshape thermal emission in metasurfaces and show that by directly controlling the
dispersion and losses of photonic bands through EPs, we can precisely control the system's critical
coupling, resulting in highly directional, spectrally pure vectorial-polarized thermal emission.
We have cited this reference in the revised manuscript (now Ref. 44) and included a discussion on EPs
to provide a more comprehensive context.

supported by non-Hermitian descriptions43,44. To date, most studies on their intriguing results have
focused on systems that rely on material loss and gain. These systems exhibit parity-time (PT)
symmetry

regimes45,46. Near an EP, the Hilbert space of the system becomes severely "skewed", rendering the
system's dynamical behavior highly sensitive to minute perturbations. This sensitivity provides a novel
approach for designing and controlling thermal emitters with extreme spatial and spectral properties…''

Reply to Reviewer #2
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The present manuscript reported the design, theoretical analysis, and experimental demonstration of a
non-Hermitian thermal metasurface capable of generating highly directional, rainbow-free, coherent
thermal emission with vectorial polarization states. The authors introduced a nonlocal metasurface
composed of a patterned Ge membrane atop a ZnS spacer and thin gold film. By applying Brillouin-
zone folding and non-Hermitian mode engineering, they hybridized Fabry–Perot modes with quasi-
guided modes, leading to the couple of symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum (BICs).
Through carefully tuning the perturbation parameter, the system undergoes exceptional point (EP)
formation, annihilation, and reformation, leading to the emergence of topological mini-flatbands that
feature steep, wavevector-sensitive radiative loss. These bands enable critical coupling at narrowly
defined angles while suppressing emission elsewhere. The authors demonstrated experimentally the
doughnut-shaped vectorial-polarized thermal emission modes within the 3–5 um window, achieving Q-
factors up to ~100 and strong directional confinement.
The results are solid in both theory and experiment. The work presents a notable conceptual and
technological advance in thermal meta-photonics by integrating non-Hermitian physics, BIC
engineering, and dissipation control. generate. The demonstration of highly coherent structured thermal
radiation will be one step closer for the potential applications in infrared optical manipulation and
micro-scale thermal imaging. I will strongly recommend for reconsideration in Nature Communications,
if the authors can address my concerns accordingly.

particularly grateful for the recognition that our results are ''solid in both theory and experiment.'' It
is also highly encouraging to receive the reviewer's appreciation of our work as a ''notable conceptual
and technological advance'' in the field of thermal meta-photonics. We concur with the reviewer’s
perspective that the demonstration of highly coherent structured thermal radiation represents a
meaningful step toward practical applications in infrared optical manipulation and micro-scale thermal

We have carefully reviewed and addressed all the specific concerns and suggestions raised by reviewer

Indeed, the symmetry-protected nature of our system and the lattice reconfiguration mechanisms—

above the light cone, and the potential for further research in these two areas. We believe this discussion
will broaden the research interests within the nanophotonic community and stimulate future
explorations of topological metasurfaces in the context of thermal photonics.

3. The 4*4 effective Hamiltonian of TCMT contains substantial physics effects, and the authors
developed a specific case of 2*2 model to discuss EP band. Can the Hamiltonian be developed another
case for BIC band or mini flat band?
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this profound suggestion regarding the effective Hamiltonian.
This allows us to clarify the physical intuition behind our choice of simplified modes.
By applying temporal coupled-mode theory (TCMT), our goal is to distill the essential physics of the
system while retaining sufficient complexity to faithfully capture the underlying non-Hermitian
phenomena. The 2×2 Hamiltonian presented in the manuscript was intentionally derived as a reduced
effective model to isolate and illustrate the non-Hermitian coupling between two specific modes near
the exceptional point (EP). This simplification is highly effective for visualizing the topological
transition and the coalescence of eigenvalues.
In contrast, the formation of bound states in the continuum (BIC) bands—particularly the symmetry-
protected, robust BICs at the Γ point—is subject to much more stringent symmetry requirements
imposed by the two-dimensional photonic crystal. In general photonic crystal systems, BICs can be
regarded as polarization singularities in two-dimensional momentum space. Reproducing such BIC
bands within a TCMT framework therefore requires the effective Hamiltonian to rigorously respect the
intrinsic lattice symmetries and multi-channel interference conditions. While TCMT can sometimes
successfully describe BICs in simpler grating-based systems, constructing a reduced-dimensional
effective Hamiltonian that accurately captures BIC bands in a general two-dimensional photonic crystal
is nontrivial.
Therefore, we find that describing the BIC bands and the mini-flatbands requires the more
comprehensive framework. The formation of these features is fundamentally rooted in the collective
interference and symmetry constraints among all four basis modes (i.e., the hybridization between the
Fabry–Pérot modes and the quasi-guided modes). While a further reduction to another case might be
mathematically feasible under certain highly specific limits, it would inevitably obscure the multi-path
interference and the non-local coupling effects that are essential for the existence and flattening of the
mini-flatbands.
Consequently, we believe that the current TCMT Hamiltonian remains the most rigorous, efficient and
physically transparent tool for capturing the BICs and mini-flatbands, as it preserves the full symmetry
and interaction landscape of the system. We hope this clarifies why we utilized the model specifically
for the EP physics while maintaining the model for the broader band analysis.

pursuit" with significant potential for applications in thermophotovoltaics and radiative cooling. We

We have taken the reviewer’s reservations regarding the novelty and the sufficiency of our experimental
data very seriously. In response, we have substantially revised the manuscript to explicitly articulate the
fundamental physics that distinguish our work from existing studies. Furthermore, we have included
additional experimental characterizations and theoretical analyses (as detailed in the responses below
and the revised Supplementary Information) to provide more robust support for our central claims.
We believe these revisions have significantly strengthened the manuscript, addressing the concerns
raised while enhancing the overall clarity and impact of the work. Detailed point-by-point responses to
each of the reviewer's comments follow below. We hope the revised version now meets the high
standards of Nature Communications.
Major Comments：
1. Novelty and relationship to Ref. 46: Ref. 46 has already demonstrated polarization vortices in thermal
emission. In the introduction, the authors imply that such vortex emission has not been realized, which
is not accurate. The authors should fairly acknowledge the prior work and clearly state what additional
physics or capabilities the present work provides beyond Ref. 46. Besides, in my opinion, achieving a
high Q factor for thermal emission at longer wavelengths is more challenging; therefore, it is not fair to
emphasize the Q factor here, given that Ref. 46 operates at much longer wavelengths (>10 um) compared
with the present work (~5 um), and the measured Q factor in this work is also not particularly high.
Our response:
We agree with Reviewer #3 about his/her comments on the pioneering work of Ref. 42 (Previously Ref.
46). We fully acknowledge that Ref. 42 represents a major milestone in demonstrating that BIC-induced
topological singularities can be harnessed for structured thermal emissions.
While Fig. 1 in our original manuscript was specifically designed to illustrate the distinction
between vectorial-polarized thermal emission from the conventional BIC system (shown in Fig.
1a) and our proposed non-Hermitian approach (shown in Fig. 1b), we recognize that the original
phrasing in the Introduction may have been ambiguous. Accordingly, we have refined the Introduction
section to mention Ref. 42 as a precedent for thermal vortex generation, ensuring its contributions are
fairly acknowledged while clearly delineating the additional physical capabilities our platform
introduces.
As established by the comparison in Fig. 1, the fundamental physics of our study represent a significant
departure from the traditional BIC regime utilized in Ref. 42:
 While Ref. 42 relies on the intrinsic scaling properties of traditional BIC modes, our work
introduces determistic non-Hermitian engineering—specifically the manipulation of
exceptional points—to transform the radiative loss landscape.
 By tailoring these non-Hermitian dynamics, we can decouple the emission properties from the
fixed dispersion of the BIC. This enables us to shift the critical coupling point significantly
closer to the point (as visualized in Fig. 1b), allowing for highly directional, rainbow-free
emission—features that remain a substantial challenge for conventional systems like the one in
Ref. 42.
We emphasize that the central contribution of this work is not the demonstration of an isolated
polarization vortex per se, but rather the integration of topological photonics with the perspective of
non-Hermitian physics to achieve controllable, application-oriented thermal emission
functionalities. Through deliberate structural design, our approach enables high-purity, doughnut-
shaped, and highly directional vectorial-polarized coherent thermal emission, addressing practical
constraints such as angular selectivity and emission purity. In this sense, our work advances beyond
proof-of-concept demonstrations toward a platform that is directly relevant for realistic thermal
photonic applications. Regarding the Q factor, we appreciate the reviewer's perspective on the inherent
challenges of the >10 μm spectral window. We agree that direction comparison off Q factors across
different wavelengths can be influenced by frequency-dependent material losses and fabrication
tolerances. Consequently, we have re-centered our discussion in the revised manuscript to focus on the
temporal coherence of the structured thermal emission. We demonstrate that our non-Hermitian
approach achieves state-of-the-art performance for vectorial-polarized emission in the 3–5 μm
atmospheric window, emphasizing that our mechanism effectively controls emission characteristics
even in the presence of substantial material absorption.
We hope this clarification helps to better distinguish our work from Ref. 42. In response to the reviewer's
comments, we have revised the manuscript to more clearly highlight the additional physics and
capabilities introduced in our study. We again thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback, which
has significantly helped improve the manuscript.

Our response:
To address the identification of critical coupling by perfect absorption, we first refer to the transmission
spectrum provided in Fig. S14 of the Supplementary Information. Thee measurement results confirm
that the bottom gold film is optically thick enough to suppress light transmission (T≈0). Consequently,
in accordance with Kirchhoff’s law (E=A) and energy conservation for an opaque system (A=1−R),
the measured thermal emission is directly complementary to the reflection (E=1−R). Thus, a peak in thermal
emission corresponds directly to a dip in reflection (critical coupling).
While the reflection can be commonly measured in the near-infrared or visible regimes, directly
measuring the reflection spectrum in the Mid-infrared with collimated incidence, however, presents a
fundamental challenge when characterizing high-Q, narrow-angle resonances using standard infrared
microscopy. As illustrated in Fig. R1, our FTIR microscope employs a high-numerical-aperture (NA)
objective to ensure a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio. This setup inherently utilizes an excitation light
cone spanning an angular range exceeding 10° and is restricted to capturing spectra centered at oblique
angles (around ∼20°).
Because the critical coupling phenomenon in our non-Hermitian system is confined to an extremely
narrow angular and spectral window, the use of such a broad excitation cone results in an angularly
averaged response. This averaging effect "washes out" the sharp spectral dip associated with critical
coupling by simultaneously exciting multiple resonances within the collection cone, making it difficult
to resolve the intrinsic critical coupling feature. Given these instrumental constraints—and supported
by the fact that transmission is negligible—we maintain that our direct angle-resolved thermal emission
measurement represents the most rigorous and reliable method for characterizing the system's
performance at highly collimated angles.
Furthermore, regarding the extraction of the real and imaginary parts of the dispersion parameters,
we agree that this would be a valuable addition. In practice, however, experimentally quantifying the
imaginary part (total loss rate) is complicated by fabrication-induced scattering losses. The sidewall
roughness introduces an extrinsic scattering loss channel that contributes to the non-radiative decay,
making it extremely challenging to distinguish intrinsic material absorption from scattering losses under
the current experimental conditions. Consequently, attempting to extract the precise complex dispersion
parameters from the experimentally broadened spectra would likely yield inaccurate results.
We hope this explanation clarifies the physical and technical rationales behind our measurement
approach and highlights the reliability of the thermal emission data presented in the manuscript.

to the absorption spectrum, or the reflectivity R(λ) calculated for each configuration, with the emissivity
subsequently determined by subtracting the reflectivity from 1.
